subject: typewriter
reasoning:
I'm planning a TypeScript module that builds a stylized typewriter from primitives using the SDK, sizing it realistically at roughly 0.45m wide, 0.35m deep, 0.17m tall, with a body box, rows of keys, a carriage and platen cylinder, and paper sheet details.

I'm sketching the skeleton hierarchy: a root "body" joint, a "carriage" child joint, and a "lever" joint with a hinge role for the return lever. For the keycaps I'm considering generating small SVG textures with letters rendered on cream-colored boxes to give each key its own label.

I realize transparent SVG backgrounds would make the keys see-through due to the cutaway effect, so I need a solid background rect behind each letter. To avoid overloading the texture atlas with dozens of letter textures, I'll simplify by skipping individual letter keys and just using plain cream boxes with a dark-red accent, saving SVG textures for the paper sheet and brand plate instead.

For the paper, I'm deciding between a box (which shows text on all faces, somewhat acceptable) versus a front-facing plane (invisible from behind) -- I'll go with a textured plane facing forward backed by a plain white box for body. For the carriage, I'm orienting the platen cylinder horizontally along the X axis using a direction parameter to remap the geometry's default Y-axis orientation.

Now I'm laying out the body structure: a main box for the chassis, small cylindrical feet at the corners for support, and a sloped keyboard panel positioned at the front-top tilted slightly forward using rotation around the X axis to simulate the angled key deck.

Working out the trig to position keys correctly on the tilted panel surface, then planning 4 rows of 10 keys with proper spacing, a wide spacebar, and a few colored shift keys to round out the keyboard layout.

For the typebasket, I'm sketching an arc of thin rod levers that pivot near the body front and reach up to strike points at the platen, connecting carriage, platen, and keys into a plausible typewriter mechanism.

Now I'm building the carriage frame with side uprights, a connecting top bar, and a cylindrical platen with small knob cylinders at the ends, along with a thin sheet for paper fed through behind the platen.

Adjusting the paper position so it sits just in front of the platen's actual front edge, then aligning the typebar strike point to land right where the platen surface meets the paper.

Now I'm thinking through the rigging: adding a hinge joint for the return lever on the carriage's right side, and setting up a parent-child joint hierarchy with body as root, carriage attached at the platen position, and the lever joint also parented to body.

For the body itself, I'm picking a color palette—deep teal body, cream keys with dark lettering, red accents on shift/return keys, and silver trim—then placing a box geometry for the main body chassis.

Still laying out parts...

Laying out keyboard rows...

Computing the world-space transform for keys given the panel's 12-degree tilt, placing them slightly above the panel surface with matching rotation so they sit flush on the tilted plane.

Checking the slope math: with the tilt, the panel surface slopes down toward the front (typical typewriter ergonomics), but that creates a clash where the front of the body box pokes above the sloped panel edge. I need to shrink the body box height so its top stays below the panel at the front.

I'll adjust body height to 0.04-0.12 so the front face aligns better with the panel, then check the rear hump box dimensions against the panel's back edge placement — close enough to call it good. Now I'm moving on to positioning the carriage uprights.

Right, the strike point needs to sit between the platen and paper, so I'll place the paper around z -0.072, sandwiched between the platen at -0.075 and the bar strike point at -0.068, keeping the geometry consistent front-to-back.

Now I'm working out the typebasket: 13 bars fanning out from pivots hidden under the panel near [x, 0.14, -0.03], rising up to strike the paper at around [x, 0.31, -0.072], spreading across x from -0.13 to 0.13.

I'm accepting that the rods will pass through the hump region stylistically, keeping it simple rather than reworking the carriage geometry, and attaching the rods to the body as their bone reference.

For the return lever, I'm positioning it on the left side with a pivot joint, then adding a rod arm extending up and back with a small red sphere knob at the end as the handle, deciding to skip extras like a ribbon spool or bell to keep things manageable.

Now I'm placing the platen knobs as small cylinders at both ends of the roller, with rubber end caps in a dark tone, plus adding a silver trim stripe across the body front and defining the color palette—teal body, cream keys, red accent, chrome, and dark panel tones. I'm also positioning a label plaque on the front face just below the panel, letting the panel's top edge overhang slightly past the body front like a classic typewriter silhouette.

Checking overall proportions against a real typewriter, then working out the feet as small cylinders under the base plate, with the silver base plate and body box dimensions aligned so the feet tuck neatly underneath. I'm defining the rear hump of the body as an angled box tucked into the main shell.

Writing the keyboard panel tilt math, computing a helper function that projects key positions onto the angled panel plane using trig based on a 12-degree tilt. Now starting the panel geometry code...

Generating the key layout, looping through rows and columns to place small cream-colored key blocks on the panel, with red accents for special keys like return and shift. Tallying up the total part count to stay well under budget, and deciding to keep keys simple without engraved letters. Now I'm writing the SVG markup for the paper texture, laying out a serif "Dear reader," heading and adjusting the viewBox to match the plane's aspect ratio.

Working out label and paper plane placement, including a typewriter nameplate SVG and attaching the paper geometry to the carriage joint with proper orientation, then setting up a lever joint connected to the body.

Now I'm figuring out the platen, carriage uprights, knobs, and typebar rods radiating from pivot points to strike positions near the panel, accepting that some rods will visually pass through the keyboard panel like real typewriters. I'm finalizing the root joint setup, feet placement at ground level, and trimming imports to only what's used before writing the final code.
